Run the first command from the directory that holds the installed copy's `scripts/`: the skill's own directory for a copy made by `npx ffmpeg-skill`, a Claude Code plugin or a copy by hand, and the plugin's top directory (the one that contains `skills/`) for the Codex plugin: ```bash python3 scripts/_contract.py doctor --json # from the directory that holds scripts/ npx ffmpeg-skill doctor --json # checks the invoked npm package, not a plugin copy ``` - **It works in my terminal but not in my agent.** Compare `ffmpeg_path` and `ffprobe_path` against the binaries seen by the agent (a copy older than 3.13.0 does not report them: update it first, see [Updating](#updating)). Use both binaries from the same build, and restart the host after changing the PATH it inherits. If the direct Python command fails, check `python3 --version` (3.10 or newer); on Windows, use `python` or `py -3` if `python3` is unavailable. - **A specific tool won't run.** In the installed copy's report, look under `tools` (for example, `tools.stabilize`) for that tool's `usable` status and any `fix` message. See [Quick start](#quick-start) for how to interpret the overall status. - **The agent still uses an older version.** Use the installed copy's `version` in the report, then follow [Updating](#updating) for that installation route. A newer version reported by the npm command doesn't establish that the agent's own copy was updated. ## Requirements - FFmpeg 6.1+ (3.0.0 removed 5.x; an older build is refused). Required by at least one tool (so `doctor`'s `ok` needs them all): `libx264`, `aac`, and the `drawtext`, `subtitles` (libass), `loudnorm`, `xfade`, `acrossfade`, `amix`, `overlay`, `scdet`, `silencedetect`, `cropdetect`, `tile`, `tpad`, `boxblur`, `hqdn3d`, `yadif`, `reverse`, `rotate`, `showwaves`, `v360`, `xstack` and `vidstabdetect`/`vidstabtransform` (libvidstab, `stabilize.py` only) filters; `doctor --json` lists them as `capabilities.required`. Needed only by the flags that use them: `libx265`, `prores_ks`, `libzimg` / `zscale`, `libmp3lame`, `libopus`, `libvorbis`, the `ass` filter. `doctor` tells you which are present. The apt and gyan.dev builds carry all of them; some Homebrew bottles lack `libass` / `libfreetype` / `libzimg`, which `doctor` reports as missing. - Python 3.10+, standard library only (3.0.0 removed 3.9) - Node 16+ only for the `npx` installer `doctor`'s own introspection calls (`ffmpeg -filters`/`-encoders`/`-bsfs`/`-version`) time out after 10s and report `failed` rather than hanging forever — those are meant to be fast. Every tool's actual media-processing `ffmpeg` invocation (cut, fit, caption, ...) runs under `--timeout` (default 1800 s, `FFMPEG_SKILL_TIMEOUT`, `0` = none): past the limit the process is killed, its partial output removed, and the failure reported as `kind: timeout` (exit 124) — a legitimately long `--accurate` re-encode should raise the limit rather than run unbounded. `-nostdin` is always passed, so a hung ffmpeg process waiting on stdin cannot happen. ## Stability 4.x splits the promise by tool: the 12 core tools (`stability: stable` in `contract --json`) keep every tool name, CLI argument, JSON output key and exit code working until 5.0, as every tool did in 3.x; the other 29 (`beta`) may drop or rename an argument or an output key in a minor release after one minor of notice in `deprecated`. The full list of what is promised and what is not, and the three-step deprecation policy, is in [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md#stability-guarantee-4x). It is enforced by a test that pins every tool's argument names against a snapshot, so a breaking change fails CI instead of slipping into a patch. Releases are batched: related fixes and features ship together as one version rather than one version per merged pull request, so a dependent project sees fewer, larger steps. Pin a tagged version, not `main`. 2.0.0 made the five changes announced since 1.10.0 -- `--crf` removed in favour of `--quality` (except on `export.py`, whose preset chooses the encoder), an existing output refused without `--overwrite`, `probe`'s `hdr` narrowed to a real HDR signal, `json`/`progress` out of the MCP schema, the `result_v2` preview withdrawn -- listed with what to change in [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md#what-20-changed) and under `removed` in `contract --json`. 3.0.0 is the second break: it removed FFmpeg 5.x and Python 3.9 (announced in 2.14.0 and 2.10.9), made `cut.py` keep an `.mp4`/`.mov` copy's edit list, keep an SDR HEVC source HEVC and use `--vfr-guard sampled` by default (`--no-edit-list`, `--no-keep-hevc` and `--vfr-guard average` restore 2.x), and changed what `cut.py`'s `precision` (now the least exact segment's) and `keyframe_snapped` (now equal to `start_snapped`) mean (`contract_version` 2.0) -- see [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md#what-30-changed). 4.0.0 is the third: it split the promise by tool (above), made `export.py` exit non-zero when a video delivery misses a required property, made `fit.py --duration` ask for `--method` before a retime beyond 1.15x, turned on content checks in the delivery templates, and gave unusable inputs their own `error.reason` -- see [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md#what-40-changed). ## Those tests, among them `test_dry_run_never_runs_ffmpeg_and_writes_nothing` and the whole `DoctorDetectionTests` class, skip there (`skipIf`, or `skipTest` inside the test) and show as `skipped`, not silently absent, in the Windows job's log; `grep -n 'os.name == "nt"\|platform.system() == "Windows"' tests/test_contract.py` finds their conditions, among the suite's other platform branches. The rest — contract schema, `reencodes_*`, `doctor.tools`, MCP derivation, and the tools exercised through the contract, including `cut.py`'s provenance fields — runs against the real Windows `ffmpeg` on every PR. See [references/ci-platform-pitfalls.md](references/ci-platform-pitfalls.md) for this and other per-OS behaviour differences already diagnosed, before spending a CI cycle re-diagnosing a platform-only failure. **Releasing** is fully automated end to end, including the version number itself — a PR never needs to touch `package.json` or the version in `docs/contract.md`. `CHANGELOG.md` is different: the release writes the version heading and one line per merged PR, but a `feat` PR writes its own notes as a fragment file under `changelog.d/` (CONTRIBUTING.md, `changelog.d/README.md`), which the release folds into the new section, and a PR that closes an issue must name that issue in `CHANGELOG.md` or `test_changelog_mentions_every_closed_issue_since_last_tag` fails. Once a PR merges to `main`, `.github/workflows/release.yml` takes it from there: if nobody bumped the version by hand, it resolves the next version with [.github/scripts/resolve_version.py](.github/scripts/resolve_version.py). What that script reads, its rules, their exceptions and the incidents behind them are written once, in its docstring, and `test_release_version_resolver_rules` and `test_release_version_resolver_does_not_depend_on_a_pr_title` pin them; they are not restated here. Most PRs don't need a label added by hand: `release-drafter.yml`'s `autolabel` job applies one automatically from the PR's title/changed files (`Fix ...` → `fix`, `Add ...`/`feat ...` → `feature`, `docs`/`.md`/`.github/`/`build(deps)` changes → `chore`) as soon as it's opened — add a label yourself only to override that. **A major version is never chosen automatically**: no label rule produces `major`, and the workflow refuses to auto-bump across a major boundary even if someone applies that label — a real major release is a deliberate `package.json` bump in a PR, which the manual path below already handles. It bumps `package.json`, `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, `docs/contract.md` and `docs/roadmap.md`'s released-version sentence, writes a `CHANGELOG.md` section listing those PRs (and any issues they closed), and pushes that commit to `main` itself. If another PR merged while the bump was being prepared, the push is refused and that run releases nothing: the newer merge's own run, queued behind it, starts from `main`'s tip and releases both (the bump is never rebased onto a merge it did not read). After the tag it also asks `pages.yml` to rebuild the site, because the bump commit carries `[skip ci]` and would otherwise leave the site on the previous version. Either way — auto-bumped or hand-bumped in the PR — it then creates the `vX.Y.Z` tag, publishes a GitHub Release with notes extracted from `CHANGELOG.md`'s matching section, and publishes the package to npm. A PR that still wants to write its own version bump and `CHANGELOG.md` prose (e.g. to explain the "why" of a release by hand) can — the automation only fills in when nobody made that call already. A push to `main` with nothing new to release creates no tag, Release or npm publish; its MCP Registry step still asks npm and the registry about `server.json`'s version and publishes the entry only when npm has that version and the registry does not, which is how a later run finishes an entry an earlier one failed to publish. npm publishing needs an `NPM_TOKEN` repo secret (an npm access token with publish rights on this package) — without it the tag and GitHub Release still happen, only the npm step is skipped. A repo that depends on this one (an editing skill, an agent) should pin an `ffmpeg-skill` version by tag or npm version, not by tracking `main` — a merged-but-not-yet-released commit on `main` can be ahead of the last published npm version for the few minutes between merge and this workflow completing. **A version that was tagged but never reached npm** (the npm step failed; a re-run of that release sees the tag and skips the publish) is finished by dispatching the same workflow on its tag: `gh workflow run release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f version=X.Y.Z`. That runs only the workflow's `recover` job. It refuses a version that is not `X.Y.Z`, has no tag, or that npm already has, and a run whose commit is not the tagged one: the npm provenance attestation names the run's commit, so it must be the commit the package is built from. It publishes with `--provenance` under the `latest` dist-tag when the version is above every stable (non-prerelease) version npm has, and under `backport` otherwise, so `latest` never moves back. Then it publishes the `plugin` branch when no commit there is for this version and the branch's tip is older, and the MCP Registry entry when the registry does not list the version (never for a `backport`). The GitHub Release is left as it is. A tag cut before the job was added (#448; every tag up to v3.6.3) has no `recover` job at its commit and cannot be recovered this way. Contributing a change: see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). ## Docs | | | |---|---| | [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) | scope, dev setup, tests, PR expectations | | [docs/roadmap.md](docs/roadmap.md) | the release history from 1.8.0, one theme per minor, each marked shipped + evaluated, shipped with eval pending, or planned; and what 2.0.0 then removes | | [docs/design-decisions.md](docs/design-decisions.md) | behaviours that look like bugs but are decisions, with rationale and the pinning test; read before filing a bug | | [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) | Contributor Covenant 2.1; reports go through the SECURITY.md channel | | [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) | how to report a vulnerability privately | | [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) | what the agent reads: workflow, request → tool map, audio-only rules, report format, pitfalls | | [references/scripts.md](references/scripts.md) | per-flag reference for every tool | | [references/scripts.md § Verdict thresholds](references/scripts.md#verdict-thresholds-what-passes) | every number behind `verified` and `check.py`'s rows (tolerances, silence levels, per-platform loudness and length), each with the constant or flag it comes from | | [references/devices.md](references/devices.md) | real-device notes (iPhone HDR, GoPro, DJI, screen recordings) | | [references/ci-platform-pitfalls.md](references/ci-platform-pitfalls.md) | per-OS ffmpeg/CI behaviour differences already diagnosed once — read before re-diagnosing a Windows/macOS-only test failure | | [references/process-pitfalls.md](references/process-pitfalls.md) | process mistakes already made once (breaking a pinned test by narrowing a capability list, retrying a git/GitHub operation this environment can't do, re-designing a fixture instead of recognising a real platform difference) — a living record, add to it whenever one recurs | | [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md) | the execution contract field by field, MCP relationship, how a planner consumes it | | [examples/README.md](examples/README.md) | natural-language requests and the commands behind them, `brand.json`, `project.json`, batch recipes | | [tests/fixtures/README.md](tests/fixtures/README.md) | captured and constructed FFmpeg listings, which is which | | [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) | what changed in each release | ## Support If this skill saves you time, you can help keep it maintained through [GitHub Sponsors](https://github.com/sponsors/kajisho5). Issues and pull requests are just as welcome. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) ffmpeg-skill runs your FFmpeg build as a separate executable. FFmpeg has its own license. Its LGPL builds can include encoders such as SVT-AV1 or VideoToolbox when available. Builds with GPL components such as libx264, libx265 or libvidstab use GPL terms. That affects the default x264/x265 encoding paths and the vid.stab filters used by `stabilize.py`. FFmpeg labels builds configured with `--enable-nonfree` as non-redistributable. `doctor` displays the license reported by the selected executable. See [FFmpeg's license and distribution information](https://ffmpeg.org/legal.html).

# Runs on every pull request and on pushes to main (workflow_dispatch stays for manual runs).
# The OSes give several FFmpeg majors: Ubuntu 24.04 apt = 6.1, Ubuntu 26.04 apt = 8.0.1, Homebrew = 8.x,
# gyan.dev on Windows = 9.x (plus the 7.1 Debian job below).
# The "ffmpeg listings" artifact holds each runner's `ffmpeg -filters / -encoders / -bsfs` output
# and `doctor --json`, so a parser regression on a new FFmpeg layout is visible in the log and the
# capture can be copied into tests/fixtures/.
name: tests
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

# A push while this is still running on the same PR/branch makes the old run pointless -- its
# result is about to be superseded anyway. Cancelling it saves real money here: this matrix
# includes macOS (10x the Ubuntu minute cost) and Windows (2x), so a few stacked pushes without
# this can burn many times the minutes of the one push that actually mattered.
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true


# the jobs only read the repository and upload artifacts; the token gets nothing else
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    # a part takes 10 to 25 minutes; a filter graph that never ends on one FFmpeg (#514) ran
    # until the six-hour default
    timeout-minutes: 75
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
        python: ["3.10"]
        # the suite on three machines at once (tests/run_parallel.py --part): about a third of the
        # wall time, and the standard runners cost nothing on a public repository
        part: [1, 2, 3]
        # The docs promise Python 3.10+ (3.0.0 removed 3.9); 3.10 is the floor and every OS runs it. One extra Linux
        # job on the newest CPython proves the ceiling too (3.11-3.12 sit between the two; a
        # stdlib-only codebase that passes on both ends is very unlikely to break in the
        # middle). Linux only: it bills at 1x, macOS at 10x. See #146.
        include:
          - {os: ubuntu-latest, python: "3.13", part: 1}
          - {os: ubuntu-latest, python: "3.13", part: 2}
          - {os: ubuntu-latest, python: "3.13", part: 3}
    # ubuntu-latest is Ubuntu 26.04, whose setup-python builds start above 3.10; keep the floor on
    # the newest image that has it (24.04, which also gives apt's FFmpeg 6.1, the FFmpeg floor)
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.python == '3.10' && startsWith(matrix.os, 'ubuntu') && 'ubuntu-24.04' || matrix.os }}
    name: test (${{ matrix.os }}, py${{ matrix.python }}, ${{ matrix.part }}/3)
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
          # Full history (not the default shallow depth-1 clone): test_contract.py's
          # test_changelog_mentions_every_closed_issue_since_last_tag walks git log back to the
          # latest tag to check CHANGELOG.md against "Closes #N" in commit bodies -- a shallow
          # clone would make that check silently a no-op (no tag reachable to diff against).
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: actions/setup-python@6d4fd22b20465ccc0f7354476588e8df7c9ca0e0 # v7.1.0
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
      - name: Install ffmpeg (Linux)
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        # the runner image's packages.microsoft.com source has answered 403 (#751, #757), which failed
        # the job before a test ran; nothing here installs from it
        run: |
          grep -l packages.microsoft.com /etc/apt/sources.list.d/* 2>/dev/null | xargs -r sudo rm -f || true
          sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y ffmpeg fonts-dejavu-core
      - name: Install ffmpeg (macOS)
        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
        # Homebrew's `ffmpeg` formula no longer links libass / freetype / harfbuzz / zimg, so it has no
        # subtitles, ass, drawtext or zscale filter; `ffmpeg-full` does. It is keg-only: put it on PATH.
        run: |
          brew install ffmpeg-full
          echo "$(brew --prefix ffmpeg-full)/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
      - name: Install ffmpeg (Windows)
        if: runner.os == 'Windows'
        # The Chocolatey community feed (community.chocolatey.org) intermittently 503s under load
        # -- seen repeatedly failing CI with nothing wrong in the PR's own diff. Retry with backoff
        # instead of failing the whole job on what's usually a transient upstream blip.
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          # A zero exit from choco is not proof ffmpeg is usable: seen once returning 0 after
          # ~6 s with nothing on PATH (the next step's `ffmpeg -version` then failed). So the
          # success condition is "ffmpeg actually runs", and a phantom install is retried with
          # --force rather than trusted.
          $attempts = 5
          for ($i = 1; $i -le $attempts; $i++) {
            $force = if ($i -gt 1) { '--force' } else { '' }
            # Pinned: the feed moved to 9.1.0 on 2026-11-20 and the same commit that passed on 9.0.2
            # then failed there (sound ending 148 samples late in grid/broll/multicam, sync and
            # verify running past their time limit). Unpin when the 9.1 report is closed.
            choco install ffmpeg --version 9.0.2 -y --no-progress $force
            $code = $LASTEXITCODE
            if ($code -eq 0 -and (Get-Command ffmpeg -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) -and (Get-Command ffprobe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
              ffmpeg -version | Select-Object -First 1
              break
            }
            if ($code -eq 0) { Write-Host "choco reported success but ffmpeg/ffprobe are not on PATH (attempt $i/$attempts)"; $code = 1 }
            if ($i -eq $attempts) { exit $code }
            $delay = 15 * $i
            Write-Host "choco install ffmpeg failed (attempt $i/$attempts, exit $code) -- retrying in ${delay}s"
            Start-Sleep -Seconds $delay
          }
      - name: ffmpeg version, listings and doctor
        shell: bash
        run: |
          mkdir -p listings
          ffmpeg -version | head -1 | tee listings/version.txt
          ffmpeg -hide_banner -filters > listings/ffmpeg_filters.txt
          ffmpeg -hide_banner -encoders > listings/ffmpeg_encoders.txt
          ffmpeg -hide_banner -bsfs > listings/ffmpeg_bsfs.txt
          head -9 listings/ffmpeg_filters.txt
          # doctor exits 1 when a required capability is missing on this build (e.g. Homebrew without libass);
          # that is reported, not hidden, but the listings must still be uploaded
          python scripts/_contract.py doctor --json > listings/doctor.json || echo "doctor exit $?"
          cat listings/doctor.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2
        if: always()
        with:
          name: ffmpeg-listings-${{ matrix.os }}-py${{ matrix.python }}-${{ matrix.part }}
          path: listings/
      # this machine's third of test_all.py's modules and test_contract, sharded across its cores.
      # A handful of test_contract tests drive the tools through POSIX shell shims (fake ffmpeg on
      # PATH) and are skipIf'd on Windows; everything else runs on all three OSes.
      - run: python tests/run_parallel.py --part ${{ matrix.part }}/3
      - run: node bin/install.js
        if: matrix.part == 1
      - name: Cross-module -k and reverse-order test isolation (Linux)
        if: runner.os == 'Linux' && matrix.part == 1 && matrix.python == '3.10'
        run: |
          python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -k font -k fonts_dir -k frozen_1x
          python3 -m unittest tests.test_picture tests.test_analysis -k fontfile -k font_flag_escapes

  # The docs promise FFmpeg 6.1+ (3.0.0 removed 5.x); the matrix above runs 6.1 (apt on Ubuntu
  # 24.04), 8.x (Homebrew) and 9.x (gyan.dev). This Linux-only (1x cost) job pins 7.1, which
  # needs a different base image altogether. See #146.
  #
  # 7.1.x: no maintained static build carries drawtext any more (John Van Sickle's 7.0.2 lacks
  # the filter; BtbN dropped 7.x), but Debian trixie's apt ffmpeg is 7.1 with libass, freetype
  # and zimg, so this job runs inside a trixie container. It also happens to give Python 3.13.
  test-ffmpeg-7:
    name: test (debian-trixie container, py3.13, ffmpeg 7.1 apt, ${{ matrix.part }}/3)
    timeout-minutes: 75
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        part: [1, 2, 3]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container: debian:trixie
    steps:
      - name: Install ffmpeg 7.1, Python, fonts, git and node
        run: |
          apt-get update -qq
          DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y -qq ffmpeg python3 fonts-dejavu-core git nodejs ca-certificates
          git config --global --add safe.directory "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: ffmpeg version, listings and doctor
        run: |
          mkdir -p listings
          ffmpeg -version | head -1 | tee listings/version.txt
          python3 --version
          ffmpeg -hide_banner -filters > listings/ffmpeg_filters.txt
          ffmpeg -hide_banner -encoders > listings/ffmpeg_encoders.txt
          ffmpeg -hide_banner -bsfs > listings/ffmpeg_bsfs.txt
          python3 scripts/_contract.py doctor --json > listings/doctor.json || echo "doctor exit $?"
          cat listings/doctor.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 # v7.0.2
        if: always()
        with:
          name: ffmpeg-listings-debian-trixie-ffmpeg7-${{ matrix.part }}
          path: listings/
      - run: python3 tests/run_parallel.py --part ${{ matrix.part }}/3   # this machine's third, test_contract included

sampled_files.README.md:
Give your coding agent a video editor.
Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client edits your footage with local FFmpeg, then checks its own output.
No cloud · No API keys · Python standard library
What you install and what it touches

Website · Quick start · Demos · Tools · MCP · npm

 

 

English · 日本語（サイト）

```bash npx ffmpeg-skill ```

caption.py --animate pop --karaoke
fit.py --aspect 9:16 --fit crop

silence.py --threshold -35
loudness.py -I -14 --tp -1


Twelve clips edited by asking: colour, slow motion and reframing, a talk laid out with its slides and cut into a captioned short, a pause removed, a green-screen composite, a levelled horizon, and three phone clips (stabilised, a night shot lifted and denoised, 60 fps slowed down). Watch them (English and Japanese) · the request and the exact commands. Nine clips are AI-generated with Google Veo; three are shot on a phone.

### Review page After an edit, ask your agent for the review page ("show me the review page"), or run `npx ffmpeg-skill review project.json --result run.json` yourself (`python3 scripts/_review.py` from a checkout). It writes one local HTML file. It shows the sources, every step with its checks, the result in a phone frame with the platform's safe area, and a timeline. Press the number of a clip or a caption, write what should change, and copy the instruction it builds back to your agent. Nothing is uploaded; the page speaks English, Japanese, Korean and Chinese.


The talk above as a vertical short, on the review page (AI-generated footage).

Left half is the input, right half is what the command produced. **[Every before/after demo, with the exact command under each one →](docs/demos.md)** — all of it built by `python3 demos/build.py`, so you can rebuild every frame of it yourself. The pictures come from [demos/footage/](demos/footage/README.md): clips AI-generated with Google Veo (the people and places do not exist) and a few shot on a phone. The sound is synthetic, and a few demos (HDR10, a panorama) use a synthetic picture. `ffmpeg-skill` is an [Agent Skill](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/agent-skills) for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and any agent that reads `SKILL.md`. It teaches the agent a fixed workflow (probe → edit losslessly where possible → check → verify) and ships **41 tools** that do the actual work with `ffmpeg` / `ffprobe`: cut, join, silence removal, fit to duration and aspect, captions and karaoke, overlays and motion graphics, HDR → SDR and LUTs, audio clean-up and typed dynamics, sync with drift correction, multicam, loudness, delivery checks, whole-edit project rendering, batch folders. Every tool is also callable as an MCP tool (`tools/list` advertises a core 12 by default to keep client context small, with `FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_FULL=1` listing all 41; every tool is reachable by name through `tools/call` either way), and the whole set is described by a machine-readable contract. If `ffmpeg` and `python3` are on your PATH, it works: offline, on footage you would rather not upload. - **Protect your source files.** A destination that matches a declared input is refused. Direct edits require `--overwrite` to replace an existing output. A `batch --watch` job can replace an unchanged file it delivered on an earlier pass. The `-y` in the dry-run command takes effect only after the tool checks the destination. - **Call typed tools.** The agent supplies named options such as `--aspect 9:16` and `--fit pad`. The tool builds the FFmpeg command and filter graph. - **Verify the edit.** The tools probe the source and the written file, so the agent can check the actual duration, frame size and audio before reporting success. > **SPEC** (Self-Producing Execution Contract): each tool's `input_schema` — the part of its > contract and MCP tool definition that has to track the CLI flag-for-flag — is never > hand-authored beside the code. It is derived, at run time, from the same `argparse` parser that > already defines the CLI, and CI fails the build if any of it drifts. > → [full explanation](#what-is-spec) --- ## Standalone, and in an ecosystem **Standalone**, this is a local FFmpeg engine: probe → edit → verify, `npx ffmpeg-skill` and nothing else. No API key, no account, no other repo required. Everything above and below this section describes that standalone tool, and none of it changes if you never read the rest of this one. **In [kajisho5](https://github.com/kajisho5)'s wider video-production ecosystem**, this repo is the *hands*: it cuts, measures and exports files, and reports back in structured JSON. It does not decide what to cut, whether a deliverable is approvable, what makes a highlight interesting, or what a caption should say (the user's cue text is burned as written, never rewritten to fit) — those are a *brain*'s job, sitting in front of this engine, not inside it. | You want to... | Use | |---|---| | Cut / join / measure / export a file right now | **this repo** (`ffmpeg-skill`), standalone | | Decide cut points, approve a deliverable, plan a whole edit | [`video-production-agent`](https://github.com/kajisho5/video-production-agent) / [`AI-video-production-OS`](https://github.com/kajisho5/AI-video-production-OS) | | Build a typed editing graph across a workspace, without writing raw `ffmpeg` | [`video-editing-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/video-editing-skill) / [`audio-production-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/audio-production-skill) | | Put Remotion motion graphics (animated captions, silence jump cuts, audio-peak motion) on a real recording | [`remotion-ffmpeg-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/remotion-ffmpeg-skill): its compositions take their length, fps, frame, silences, scene cuts, audio peaks and beats from this repo's `probe.py`, `silence.py` and `scenes.py`. It verifies its render with `check.py` and `look.py`, composites a graphics layer with `overlay.py` (`--place` for its `--sparse` mode), and delivers through `render.py --template` | Other repos in the ecosystem — [`media-analysis-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/media-analysis-skill), [`transcription-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/transcription-skill), [`subtitle-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/subtitle-skill), [`thumbnail-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/thumbnail-skill), [`color-grading-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/color-grading-skill), [`motion-graphics-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/motion-graphics-skill), [`qc-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/qc-skill) — read this repo's `contract --json`, its tools' `--json` output and `doctor`, the same way any agent framework would; this repo does not call into any of them. The dependency runs one way. --- **Contents** [Standalone, and in an ecosystem](#standalone-and-in-an-ecosystem) · [Why](#why) · [Quick start](#quick-start) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Design principles](#design-principles) · [Tools](#tools) · [Audio](#audio-is-a-first-class-input) · [Built for agents](#built-for-agents) · [FAQ](#faq) · [FFmpeg compatibility](#ffmpeg-compatibility) · [Tested on real footage](#tested-on-real-footage) · [Install](#install) · [Requirements](#requirements) · [Development](#development) · [Docs](#docs) --- ## Why An agent that "knows FFmpeg" still guesses: it assumes a frame rate, picks a codec the container cannot hold, re-encodes a file that only needed a stream copy, and reports "done" without opening the result. This skill takes the guessing out: - **Real files first.** Every job starts with `probe.py`; the agent decides from the measured duration, fps, resolution, colour and audio layout, not from the file name. - **Structured tools, not shell strings.** Each operation is a script with typed arguments. Nothing runs through a shell; no filter graph is accepted from the caller. - **A contract the agent can read.** `contract --json` states, for every tool, what it takes, what it writes, which FFmpeg components it needs and how the result is verified. The MCP surface is derived from it. - **Verification after execution.** The result is probed, checked against the destination's spec and, when the picture changed, looked at as a contact sheet. - **Local first.** No cloud, no API keys, no Python dependencies. Optional local transcription is used when a speech engine (Parakeet or a whisper) is installed, never required — by `caption.py --transcribe` and, since 1.17, by `silence.py --transcribe` (with `--filler`, or since 3.6 with `--sentence-min-silence` / `--sentence-margin-tail`); both take a transcript you already have instead, and both refuse with the install lines rather than guessing. Both take `--engine` and `--model`; `FFMPEG_SKILL_ASR_ENGINE` and `FFMPEG_SKILL_ASR_MODEL` set this machine's defaults (e.g. `large-v3-turbo` where that whisper.cpp model is installed; without either, auto and `base`). The engine runs on your machine and the audio is never uploaded; parakeet-mlx, faster-whisper and openai-whisper download their model weights the first time they run (parakeet-mlx's default from Hugging Face). ## Paper The design discipline behind this skill — per-operation verification for AI agents — is written up as a position paper. The paper scores ffmpeg-skill itself as only partially conformant with the discipline it defines. Kajiyama, S. (2026). *What Is Verification-Driven Coding? — A Discipline for Not Trusting Generation.* Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23720216 ## Quick start One command does steps 0 to 2 below: `npx ffmpeg-skill setup` installs the skill for every agent it finds on the machine (`~/.claude`, `~/.cursor`, `~/.codex` or `~/.agents`; Claude Code when it finds none), installs FFmpeg when `ffmpeg` does not run (`brew install ffmpeg-full`, `winget install --id Gyan.FFmpeg -e` or `sudo apt-get install -y ffmpeg`, printed before it runs; `--no-ffmpeg` never runs a package manager), and ends with `doctor`, whose exit status it returns. On a system with none of those three package managers it installs the skill, says FFmpeg is still missing, and exits non-zero. It needs Node 16+ and Python 3.10+, and installs neither. ```bash npx ffmpeg-skill setup ``` The same steps one at a time: ```bash # 0. FFmpeg itself, once (Ubuntu/Debian shown; macOS and Windows are in the Install table below) sudo apt install ffmpeg # 1. install the skill for Claude Code (Cursor: --cursor, Codex: --codex, all three: --all) npx ffmpeg-skill # 2. check the machine: ffmpeg, ffprobe and every FFmpeg component the tools need npx ffmpeg-skill doctor # 3. (for agent frameworks) read the machine-readable contract npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json | head -40 ``` Captions from speech (`caption.py --transcribe`) need one local speech engine, installed separately. `pip install faster-whisper` is the simplest; the first run downloads its model, and the audio never leaves the machine. Without an engine, everything else works, `doctor` lists the engine as missing optional, and `--transcribe` refuses with the install line for each engine it supports. Already installed? re-run `npx ffmpeg-skill` to refresh `~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill`. Copies are not updated automatically. `doctor`'s overall `ok` and a single tool's `usable` are different signals: `ok` is false when anything *some* tool requires is missing, so one missing filter (a plain Homebrew `ffmpeg` without `subtitles`, or a build without libvidstab) turns it false even though most tools still run. Check `doctor --json`'s `tools` field for the per-tool answer, not just `ok`. Then talk to your agent: > "Take `interview.mp4`, keep 0:45–1:20 and 5:00–5:25, and make it a 60-second Reel." The agent runs `probe.py`, `cut.py --segments 0:45-1:20,5:00-5:25 --accurate`, `fit.py --aspect 9:16 --fit crop`, `export.py --preset reels`, `check.py --platform reels` and `look.py`, then reports "final.mp4: 60.00 s, 1080×1920, 30 fps, AAC stereo" with the contact sheet it inspected. ### Deliver to a platform One command per destination, with the app's own UI taken into account: ```bash python3 $S/render.py talk.mp4 --template tiktok --cues cues.txt ``` That fills the shipped `templates/tiktok.json`: 9:16 crop, captions popped word by word *above* TikTok's description bar and clear of its like column, −14 LUFS, the `tiktok` export preset, and a `check.py --platform tiktok` on the file it wrote. The caption size comes from the delivery table, so since 1.17.1 the filled project also states `"fit_size": "on"`: a size nobody asked for shrinks to fit the cue instead of splitting the sentence across two cues. A template that states its own `fit_size`, and a `--brand` that states a caption size, still win, and a project with `"fit_size": "off"` renders the captions 1.17.0 rendered. Templates ship for `tiktok`, `reels`, `shorts`, `youtube-shorts`, `youtube`, `x`, `linkedin`, `facebook`, `podcast` and `audiogram`; `--template all` (or a comma-separated list) renders the seven video destinations (`tiktok`, `reels`, `shorts`, `youtube`, `x`, `linkedin`, `facebook`) from the same edit and writes a `_pack.md` table of what each one produced. Files land next to the input unless `-o` says otherwise, and `--dry-run` shows every planned command rather than a result. `render.py --list-templates` prints them with their frames, limits and safe zones. Alias spellings work everywhere a platform is named (`youtube-shorts` = `shorts`, `ig` = `reels`, `twitter` = `x`, `fb` = `facebook`). The tools also work on their own, from any shell: ```bash S=~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill/scripts python3 $S/probe.py input.mp4 --compact python3 $S/fit.py input.mp4 --duration 60 --method trim --aspect 9:16 --dry-run # plan a trim and reframe python3 $S/export.py input.mp4 --preset reels --json # structured result with a probe of the output ``` On Windows in Git Bash, `python3` is only on PATH if Python was installed from the Microsoft Store; a python.org install exposes `python` (or the `py` launcher) instead — replace `python3` with `python` above if you see a "command not found". `bin/install.js` and `doctor`/`contract` already handle this for you; only the raw script examples above need it spelled out manually. A test copies the skill, adds, removes and edits a script, and reads `tools/list` again to prove it. ## Design principles These are the rules the skill file gives the agent and the code enforces. 1. **Probe first.** No tool decides from the file name. `probe.py` measures duration, fps (with variable-frame-rate detection), resolution, rotation, bit depth, HDR format including Dolby Vision, colour tags and every audio stream before anything is cut. 2. **Lossless when possible.** `cut.py` and `loudness.py` stream-copy what they do not need to touch (`join.py` re-encodes so it can crossfade and conform mismatched clips; `--copy --transition none` joins clips that already match by stream copy). Re-encoding happens only when it must: frame-accurate cuts, filters, format changes, or a keyframe farther than the tolerance. 3. **Plan before render.** Every tool takes `--dry-run` (print the ffmpeg command lines, write nothing; `verify` ignores it), `--plan FILE` (the dry run saved as a plan with fingerprinted inputs that `render.py FILE` executes later, refusing if an input changed; `render` and `verify` refuse it), `--json` (structured result with a probe of the output), `--fast` (preview quality), `--progress` (percent and ETA), `--timeout` (a hung ffmpeg is killed and reported, never waited on forever; Ctrl-C or SIGTERM likewise stops the running ffmpeg, removes its partial output and reports `kind: interrupted`) and `--overwrite` (explicit consent before an existing output is replaced). A test runs every tool whose contract says its dry run runs no ffmpeg (`ffmpeg_execution: none`, plus `cut` and `metadata` without their measuring flags) under `--dry-run` behind a fake ffmpeg and asserts that no ffmpeg call happened and no file appeared; another runs every tool the contract says supports `--dry-run` (all but `verify`) behind an ffmpeg that logs each decode, and asserts that no file appeared and that every tool that decoded is one the contract lists as `analysis_only`. 4. **Machine-readable contract.** `contract --json` describes all 41 tools (and `crop`, an alias of `fit --rect` since 4.19, marked `alias_of`): input schema generated from the parser, output schema, role, required and conditional FFmpeg capabilities, dry-run support, the verification tools to run afterwards, whether a visual check is required, `mutates_input: false`. `provides` lists them by a cross-repository Capability id (`ffmpeg-skill.cut`, `ffmpeg-skill.loudness`, ...) for [`kajisho5/AI-video-production-OS`](https://github.com/kajisho5/AI-video-production-OS)'s `CapabilityContract.provides` — see `docs/contract.md`. 5. **Contract-derived MCP.** `mcp/server.py` builds its `tools/list` from the contract. Tool names, order and `inputSchema` cannot drift from the scripts; a test keeps the two byte-identical. 6. **Capability detection.** `doctor` reads `ffmpeg -encoders / -decoders / -filters / -bsfs` and reports which of the components the tools need are present on this build (libx264, libass, zscale, loudnorm, xfade, …), before a job fails inside ffmpeg. 7. **Unknown is not missing.** When a listing cannot be read (a layout the parser does not know, ffmpeg exiting non-zero) the affected capabilities are `unknown`: never `missing`, never silently `available`. An installed filter is not reported absent; a failed detection is not a pass. 8. **Verify the result.** The output is probed, and when the picture changed (captions, overlays, crops, colour, transitions) the agent runs `look.py` and inspects the PNG. The report is not finished until its `Look:` line names that image; audio-only jobs say `Look: not needed`. **"Inspects" means the calling agent's own vision, not a feature of this skill:** `look.py` only renders a PNG; nothing in this repository detects faces, products, subjects, or "the interesting part" of a frame or a scene. When a crop or reframe needs to keep a specific part of the frame (`fit.py --fit crop --crop-x/-y`, see [Tools](#tools)), it is the multimodal agent looking at that PNG and choosing the anchor — a non-visual caller (a script, a CLI user without eyes on the sheet) has to supply that decision itself, and the default is a plain centre crop. Likewise `scenes.py --highlights` ranks candidate scenes by a measured proxy (`--rank-by audio` or `--rank-by duration`), never by content; it is the agent that turns a look at the sheet into a judgement. 9. **One label per report.** A finished job is `Done:`, a failure or a refusal is `Failed:`, and a partial result is `Done:` with the shortfall named in `Notes:` — never a third label such as `Done (partially):`. 10. **Keep originals.** No tool overwrites its input. Outputs are new files named `_.` unless told otherwise, and a test hashes every input after the run. ## Tools 41 public tools, all Python 3.10+ standard library, all with `--help`, `--dry-run`, `--json`, `--plan FILE` (a dry run written as a plan `render.py` executes later), non-zero exit and a reason on stderr on failure. `--json-brief` (1.11.0) prints the same result document trimmed to what a caller acts on — status, output, `verified`, a compact `summary` of the output probe, the tool's own keys and the command count instead of the command lines — for roughly a third of the bytes; `--json` itself is unchanged.
